HIGGSFIELD vs RUNWAY
Two AI Video Powerhouses. But Which One Is Actually Worth Paying For?
I've been comparing Higgsfield and Runway, and something became obvious.

The biggest difference isn't necessarily the quality of a single generated video.

It's how much control you have over the entire production process.

Both platforms can generate impressive AI footage. Both offer multiple creative capabilities.

But their strengths aren't identical.

Here's what I found.

01 — VIDEO GENERATION QUALITY

Higgsfield operates as a multi-model creative platform.

You can access video models such as Seedance 2.5, Kling, and Veo, depending on your subscription and available features.

Its advantage is flexibility.

If one model struggles with a particular scene, you can experiment with another without rebuilding your production workflow.

Runway takes a more editing-oriented approach.

Its Gen-4.5 model supports text-to-video and image-to-video generation, with detailed control through prompts describing camera movement, scene composition, and event timing.

Runway also offers third-party models, including Seedance 2.5.

Verdict: Neither platform has a universal advantage in raw generation quality. When both use the same underlying model, the prompt, settings, references, and generation workflow matter more than the platform's name.

02 — CINEMATIC CONTROL

This is where the differences become more interesting.

Higgsfield is particularly attractive for creators producing advertisements, product videos, cinematic effects, and social media campaigns.

Its creative tools emphasize camera movement, visual consistency, and production-oriented workflows.

Runway provides a different kind of control.

Its Edit Studio, powered by Aleph 2.0, allows creators to modify existing footage using instructions.

Runway's Act-Two also supports performance-driven character animation.

If I were creating multiple advertising concepts quickly, I'd investigate Higgsfield first.

If I were refining existing footage and experimenting with performance-based animation, I'd investigate Runway.

03 — COST: WHICH ONE GIVES YOU MORE?

Here's where I'd be careful.

Both platforms use credit-based pricing.

Runway's Standard plan includes 625 monthly credits.

Its Gen-4.5 model currently costs 12 credits per generated second.

That means a ten-second generation consumes 120 credits before considering retries or additional editing operations.

Higgsfield's credit consumption depends on the selected model, resolution, duration, and generation settings.

Some plans also provide temporary unlimited access to selected models.

But don't confuse unlimited access to one model with unlimited access to the entire platform.

The correct cost comparison is:

Total Production Cost ÷ Number of Approved Videos

Not simply monthly subscription price.

If one platform requires eight generations to produce an acceptable clip and another requires three, the cheaper subscription might become the more expensive workflow.

04 — AI AGENTS AND AUTOMATION

Higgsfield increasingly positions itself as a multi-model production environment, with agent-oriented workflows and integrations.

Runway also provides workflow tools, AI editing capabilities, and production automation.

But the number of available AI models isn't the same as the number of autonomous agents.

A video model generates footage.

An agent plans and executes tasks using tools.

Those are different capabilities, and they shouldn't be counted as interchangeable features.

05 — WHICH PLATFORM WOULD I ACTUALLY CHOOSE?

For cinematic product advertisements and rapid experimentation across multiple generation models:

Higgsfield.

For prompt-driven editing, performance capture, and workflows centered on modifying existing footage:

Runway.

For accessing Seedance 2.5 specifically:

Compare the cost and available controls on both platforms before subscribing.

For a serious commercial video-production workflow:

I'd run the same storyboard through both platforms.

Same reference images.

Same output specifications.

Same target duration.

Then evaluate:

→ Visual consistency
→ Motion quality
→ Prompt adherence
→ Editing flexibility
→ Audio quality, where supported
→ Generation time
→ Cost per approved clip

That's how you get a meaningful comparison.
MY TAKE
Higgsfield is particularly compelling as a multi-model creative production hub.
Runway is particularly compelling for its native generation and editing workflows.
Neither is automatically superior at every video-production task.
And there's something worth remembering before paying for either.
The best AI video platform isn't necessarily the one that generates the most beautiful five-second demo.

It's the one that can repeatedly turn your creative direction into usable footage without exhausting your budget.

That's the difference between impressive AI generation and a reliable production workflow.

In June 2025, during Game 3 of the NBA Finals, Kalshi ran a TV ad full of chaos to say the least: a farmer floating in a pool of eggs, an alien drinking beer, a man in an American flag shouting about Indiana. Its director, PJ Accetturo, made it with Google's Veo 3 for about $2,000, and it went from idea to air in three days. Production companies had quoted Kalshi "six or seven figures." It took him 300 to 400 generations to get 15 usable clips.
Ten months later, OpenAI closed the Sora app, its TikTok-style feed of AI-generated video, on 26 April. TechCrunch, drawing on a Wall Street Journal investigation, reported that the app was costing around $1 million a day to run, and that its users had fallen from a peak of about a million to fewer than 500,000. The Sora developer API followed in September, and OpenAI's price list for developers now shows no video model at all.
Together those two stories sum up video AI in 2026. Making video with AI has become cheap enough to change how ads get made. Watching AI video for its own sake hasn't turned into a business.
Video AI is already a real business: the companies that disclose revenue earn about $2.3 billion a year between them, and the customers they name are marketers, creators and businesses. It is not a small copy of the language-model market: a minute of video costs thousands of times a minute of text, and the biggest earners are apps, not model makers. The first industries hit are the ones that buy good-enough video in bulk: stock footage, ads, training and short drama. Film effects come next. Games and robots come last, and they depend on physics, where the best model today scores about half of what real footage does.
The scoreboard
 
A handful of companies now disclose their revenue, and the numbers are growing fast:
Higgsfield went from $200M → $700M ARR from end of 2025 to August 2026.
Kling, the video model from the Chinese short-video company Kuaishou, earned >$118M in the second quarter, up more than 2x on a year earlier.
fal, which acts as a bookshelf for video and image models, reached ~$400M ARR by March 2026, doubling from its level in October.
HeyGen passed $200M ARR in June.
Runway passed $200M ARR in September.
The visible total comes to about $2.3 billion a year by our calculation. Some of it is image revenue, and some is counted twice, since apps buy from fal as well. It also leaves out Google’s Veo, ByteDance’s Seedance and several Chinese labs, which don’t break out video revenue. The errors run both ways: image revenue and double counting push the total up, and the missing labs push it down. So treat $2.3 billion as a marker of scale, not a measured market size.
Not a small language model
 
Video AI is often described informally as the language-model market but a few years behind. The numbers disagree here as the delta between running a language model compared to an image/video model is very different. In simple words a language model writes the way a person types: one word at a time, each word a small guess about what comes next, and you can start reading while it is still writing. An image or video model works more like an architect. It starts from a block of random static and refines the whole picture over and over, often 20 to 50 passes, until a clear image emerges. Every pass works on every pixel at once, and nothing is usable until the last pass is done. Video multiplies that work: one second is about 24 pictures, and each one has to agree with the ones before it, so a cup stays in the same place and a face stays the same face. A paragraph of text is a few hundred small pieces, that is why one measured open model needed about 350 seconds of chip time for each second of video, and why a minute of video costs thousands of times more than a minute of text.
Anthropic told investors its annualised revenue reached $65 billion at the end of July, and OpenAI's was about $40 billion. Those two labs alone earn about 45 times the visible video total.
In language models the labs earn most of it. The largest app, the coding tool Cursor, was reported at about $4 billion a year in June, about a sixteenth of Anthropic's figure. In video the biggest earner is an app. Higgsfield's $700 million is the leader and apps that package other companies' models (Higgsfield, HeyGen, Synthesia, Magnific) make up more than half of the visible total. A text customer buys the model's intelligence and uses it directly. A video customer buys a finished clip for a job, and the clip needs editing, consistency and a workflow around it, and this is where the apps are built, creating a video workspace.
Video vs language models
A picture is worth about a thousand words
 
Until 22nd of October, the cheapest recorded price for a minute of video is about ~$3 from Veo’s cheapest tier, and the gap between the top tier was about 7,600 times.
A couple differences to notice would be that code, the biggest market for language models, can be checked automatically whereas video is judged by eye, making it subjective. Text is bought by the token; video by the clip, against a production budget.
Who is paying
Higgsfield calls itself a platform "for creators, marketers, brands, agencies, and studios" and says it "powers visual production for 390 of the Fortune 500" (Higgsfield). HeyGen says 85% of the Fortune 100 use it (HeyGen). Neither company splits its revenue by use, so nobody can say from public data how much comes from people making video for fun. All of the published evidence points to business buyers.
Split the buyers more and the business models diverge. People will watch a lot of AI video, but they pay for different things and need different quality.
Short-drama apps sell the story, episode by episode, so quality keeps viewers paying. Their biggest cost is finding viewers, not making shows: ReelShort, the largest, spent 55% of its $785 million of 2025 revenue on user acquisition and marketing, Media Partners Asia estimates (Indian Television). With 55% of revenue going to marketing, every other cost, generation included, has to fit in the remaining 45%. So a cheaper model can only trim the smaller part of the budget. A better model works on the part that earns money: whether viewers keep paying for the next episode. ReelShort does not disclose what it spends on generation, so this is our reading of the cost structure, not a measured split.
Viewers find these shows on social feeds (89% of Indian viewers in a Meta and Ormax survey), and studios are switching fast: about two-thirds of vertical-drama releases outside China in the third quarter were AI-generated, up from 3% in the first, on Owl & Co's count (The Hollywood Reporter).
AI companion apps sell an emotional connection, not a picture. Users come back for the relationship, so the video only has to be good enough. What matters is cost and speed, because each user needs a lot of video.
Cheap to make is not the same as watched
Music got here first, on the streaming service Deezer, fully AI-generated tracks passed half of all new uploads on peak days in June, and nearly 90,000 now arrive each day, the company says. They account for 1% to 3% of streams.
 
Deezer keeps detected tracks out of its recommendations and playlists, which made that gap visible. But the shape is the one the economist Herbert Simon described in 1971: when information becomes abundant, attention becomes the scarce thing. When making something becomes nearly free, supply floods, and the value moves to whoever decides what gets seen. Two researchers call the quality bar audiences set for AI content the slop ceiling.
Which industries feel it first
 
Today's $2.3 billion is small next to what is already spent on video, and the money will not move evenly. Ranked by how much of their video work today's models can already do:
Stock footage and images. A generated clip is a direct substitute for a licensed one. The two largest libraries, Getty Images and Shutterstock, had about $2 billion of revenue between them last year, this is the most exposed vertical as of today.
Ad and product video. WPP Media expects global ad revenue of about $1.3 trillion this year. Only a slice of that pays for making ads, but the Kalshi spot shows how far that slice can shrink as generation becomes cheaper cutting down on a lot of overhead that comes with producing ads in real life.
Training and explainer video. American organisations spent $102.8 billion on training in 2025 (Training magazine). This is HeyGen's and Synthesia's market, and a presenter reading a script is the easiest kind of video to generate.
Short drama. In China, revenue from micro-dramas, series of one- or two-minute episodes made for phones, was forecast to reach $9.4 billion in 2025 and overtake the country's cinema box office. These studios already accept phone-grade footage and need a lot of it.
Visual effects. IMARC puts the market at about $11 billion in 2025 (IMARC), though estimates vary widely. Studios are already using generated shots (below).
Film and TV. Ampere Analysis puts global content spending at $255 billion in 2026. AI reaches it shot by shot, not film by film.
Games and robots. Games brought in $201.6 billion in 2025, Newzoo estimates. Video models only matter here if they learn to simulate worlds, which is the last section of this piece.
What AI did to the cost of making video
 
The clearest effect so far is on cost. Beyond the Kalshi ad, Critterz, an animated feature backed by OpenAI, was budgeted at under $30 million with a nine-month schedule, against a typical $100–200 million and about three years for a major animated film.
List prices are falling by tier, not across the board.
 
The next cut is already visible in research. A measured study by Hugging Face researchers found that a large open model took 1,875 seconds on a flagship GPU to make a 5.4-second clip, which is about 350 seconds of computing per second of video by our calculation. Distillation attacks that directly. One team made a small open model turn out about 22 times more frames per second, fast enough to stream in real time on a single chip. That is where the big cost cut companion apps need would come from, at low resolution first, but then upscaled.
The price of a generated second is only part of the cost. Kalshi’s ad director kept about one clip in every 20 to 27, so for him a usable second cost 20 to 27 times the list price. That is the high end. A video-tool vendor's write-up of other productions reports one clip in four kept on a three-minute animated episode (41 of 164). Nobody has published an independent set of keep rates. Consistency works on this number directly. A model that keeps a character, a product or a camera move the same from take to take needs fewer draws, and half the draws means half the cost of a usable second. A price cut only makes each draw cheaper.
Our test: one prompt, three models. On 2 November we gave three models the same prompt through Runway's API: a phone on a glass desk lights up with a call, buzzes toward the edge, falls and bounces once on a concrete floor. Each clip was 8 seconds at 720p without sound, one take per model, $4.80 in all.
 
Left to right → Wan 3.0, Seedance 2.5, Veo 3.1.
Wan 3.0 ($0.80, first on the leaderboard) did best. The phone creeps forward, falls and settles, though the camera tilts down to follow it.
Seedance 2.5 ($2.40, the most expensive of the three) buzzes most convincingly, then cuts to a new shot just before the fall, and the screen goes dark.
Veo 3.1 ($1.60 without sound, 22nd on the leaderboard) starts with the phone standing up rather than lying flat, and bounces several times like rubber. Its screen text is the clearest of the three. (We follow Veo because Google published the clearest price history, not because it leads. On quality it now trails cheaper models, as our test also found.)
None of the three followed the whole prompt, and each took two to four and a half minutes to make, 15 to 34 times the length of the clip (our calculation). Three clips prove little, but the order matched the leaderboard, not the price.
The next turning point: cost and latency
Cheaper models are one route. The other is to copy how film and animation are already made: rough first, polished last.
Draft cheap, render once.
It’s interesting to see how animators solved this problem decades ago. They don’t animate a scene until the story works, so they sketch it first as storyboards, then as rough moving drafts called animatics. AI video can work the same way. A rough cut at one or two frames a second is enough to judge the story and the shots, like a comic strip - and the shots that make the cut and fit the best are sent to the best model for rendering.
This also fixes the keep-rate problem above. If most takes get thrown away, it’s better to throw them away while they’re cheap.
ByteDance has now built this into a product. Seedance 2.5’s Draft mode, available on fal since 30 October, makes a quick low-resolution preview and then finishes the same video in full HD. Only the keepers pay full price. The difference adds up fast (fal):
Preview (480p): about $0.22 a second
Full HD (1080p): about $1.16 a second, roughly 5 times more
Finishing a draft: fal lists no price. In our team’s test it cost 6 to 8 times less than making the clip in full HD from the start
The catch is quality. The finished draft looked a little softer than a clip made in full HD from scratch, though it also fixed an odd last frame in the preview. Scaled up, the saving is large. If 1 in 25 takes is kept (a 4% keep rate), one finished hour of full-HD video costs:
Full HD every time: about $105,000
Draft first, then finish the keepers: about $20,000 (our calculation)
The hybrid pipeline is already here.
Drafting cheaply is one shortcut. Another is to mix old tools with new ones. Creators now block out a scene in Blender, a 3D design tool, as plain grey shapes, and use OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to place the objects and the camera. They turn a still from that scene into a realistic first frame, and Seedance 2.5 brings it to life as footage (Kapwing tutorial, ByteDance’s Dreamina).
Each tool covers the other’s weakness. 3D alone was too slow to make look real, and AI video alone was hard to control. Together, the 3D draft sets the layout and the camera, and the video model supplies the look.
Real time is arriving.
The last step is speed. Video that renders while you watch is no longer a lab demo:
Runway Characters (March): a video model you can hold a live conversation with, built on Runway’s GWM-1 (Runway)
Runway Solaris (31 August): the first of what Runway calls “Interface World Models” (Crypto Briefing)
Decart (May): turns live video streams into generated scenes on the fly; raised $300 million at about a $4 billion valuation (bne IntelliNews)
Zoom avatars: realistic avatars that replace your camera feed and copy your expressions as you talk, depending on plan and region (Zoom)
Once video can be made as fast as a live call needs it, the problem for companion apps changes. It stops being how much each minute costs and becomes how fast the next frame arrives.
Beyond marketing: film, TV and effects
 
Hollywood is testing whether video AI can move beyond ads.
So far, studios have used it in two ways. They use it to make shots their budgets could never cover, and they license their characters so they get paid when others use them.
First, the shots nobody could afford.
Two recent shows used AI for scenes that would otherwise have been cut:
Netflix, The Eternaut: an Argentine series that used generative video for a building collapse. Co-chief executive Ted Sarandos said the shot was finished ten times faster than with traditional effects, at a cost that “wouldn’t have been feasible” on that budget.
Amazon, House of David: the biblical drama used 350 to 400 AI-generated images in its second season, up from about 70 in its first (TheWrap). Its showrunner said he couldn’t otherwise afford the battle scenes.
Other studios are going further and partnering with the model makers. Lionsgate took an undisclosed stake in Runway in June and plans a short-form series built on its own film library (Runway). AMC Networks has also signed with Runway (Hollywood Reporter).
Second, getting paid for the characters.
The bigger fight is over who owns the characters. Disney shows both sides of it:
June 2025: Disney and Universal sued Midjourney for copyright infringement.
December 2025: Disney agreed to invest $1 billion in OpenAI and license more than 200 of its characters for Sora (Disney).
After Sora closed: the deal ended with it, and Disney said it would look for other AI partners (Blooloop).
The message is simple: studios want to be paid for their characters, and they will sue anyone who uses them without paying.
Japan’s rights holders have moved the furthest, from blocking AI to licensing to it, and the money explains why. Anime sells well abroad, yet many of the studios that make it struggle:
¥2.17 trillion earned abroad in 2024, more than at home, on the Association of Japanese Animations’ preliminary count (gamebiz)
34.6% of anime production companies lost money in 2025 (Teikoku Databank via GameBusiness)
In October 2025, CODA, the body that represents Japanese rights holders, asked OpenAI to stop training Sora 2 on its members’ work without permission (Automaton).
Less than a year later, the tone had changed. On 11 September, the Chinese AI lab MiniMax and the Japanese firm KAGAMIAI launched H3 IP Edition in Tokyo. It lets creators make videos with licensed Japanese characters, and each character comes with approved assets, usage rules, commercial terms and reporting back to the owner. MiniMax says more than 60 companies have shown interest (MiniMax).
An earlier KAGAMIAI trial with Captain Tsubasa, run on another Chinese video model, PixVerse, shows how big the demand could be (same MiniMax page):
About 126,000 creators
About 330,000 pieces made in 45 days
More than 99% of the activity from outside Japan
Licensed fan creation could become the first mass consumer market for AI video where the owner of the characters gets paid.
The pattern is that AI can handle effects but not long projects.
Across all of these, AI handles the shots a mid-budget show could never afford: wide shots, crowds, destruction and settings. The rest of the production is still made by people. Computer graphics spread through film the same way, one effect at a time, long before Toy Story showed in 1995 that a whole feature could be made with them.
One test result points the same way. On the physics benchmark described below, the model Odyssey-3 Pro scores differently depending on where it starts:
Continuing real footage: 63, in a single attempt
Starting from a single image: 50
AI video does better when it has something real to build on, which is exactly the situation in effects work, where each generated shot sits inside real footage. The test does not measure length. No one has published a test of whether a model stays consistent across many shots, and that is the test that would explain why long projects are still out of reach.
Will specialised labs emerge?
They already have to be fair - and three kinds of video company are pulling apart:
The generalist giants. Google (Veo), ByteDance (Seedance) and Kuaishou (Kling) have the most computing power and data. They compete on quality and price, and most apps resell their models.
The studio-labs. Runway, now part-owned by Lionsgate, is building for film and TV. Moonvalley trained its Marey model only on licensed footage and had raised $154 million by July 2025. Its studio arm, Asteria, makes films with it. These labs sell three things the giants find harder to offer: training data a studio's lawyers will accept, fine control over every frame, and tools that fit into an existing effects pipeline.
The app layer. Higgsfield, HeyGen and Magnific package other labs' models for a particular customer.
The new labs, and what they are betting on. The biggest 2026 bets we found went to labs building interactive or world models: AMI Labs’ $1.03 billion seed, Runway’s $315 million raise (which it said would fund world models) and AMD’s $8.2 billion deal for World Labs. We have not totalled all video funding for the year, and the table below mixes funding rounds, one acquisition and product updates:
 
The likeliest breakthroughs in the next 12 months follow from that list: video generated live enough for calls and games, interactive worlds rather than fixed clips, and licensed-character generation at scale.
For film and effects work, the studio-lab looks most likely to win. A studio can't risk a lawsuit over a hero shot, needs to match a director's intent exactly, and works with unionised crews; a generalist that only offers the best raw model competes on price.
The bigger prize is worlds, not clips
The largest market for video models may not be video at all at the end of this intelligence run. A model that can predict the next frame of a scene may be learning how the world moves, and that would be useful for games and robots.
Runway released GWM-1 in December 2025. It calls it a general world model, in three versions: explorable worlds, conversational avatars and a robotics model that predicts what a robot's cameras will see after each action. It generates frames in real time at 720p, for up to two minutes. When it raised $315 million at a $5.3 billion valuation in February, it said the money would go towards more capable world models.
If you have read the Republic by Plato, he described this bet first in the cave.
The prisoners see only shadows on a wall, and they give honours to whoever is “quickest to observe the passing shadows” and best able to say which comes next. A video model is a prize-winning predictor of shadows that has never seen the objects casting them. Plato’s point was that this skill is not knowledge. For video models, the question is whether predicting the next frame means understanding how the world moves, and Physics-IQ is one way to test it.
 
Physics-IQ, a benchmark hosted by Google DeepMind, shows a model the start of a filmed physical event and scores how closely its continuation matches what really happened. A score of 100 means as close as a second real take. On the original scoring the best single image-to-video model has gone from 23 in February 2025 to 44 this May. On the re-scored board the leading single image-to-video entry is at 51, and Google's Veo 3.1 Fast (30) sits level with an open model from 2024 (32). The paper's own finding was that physical understanding is unrelated to how real a clip looks.
Looking real is mostly solved. Behaving real is not: the best entry still sits about halfway between zero and a second real take on this test. And because realism and physics turned out to be unrelated, better-looking clips will not close the gap by themselves.
If that score moves toward 100, video labs become simulation companies selling to game studios and robot makers, a market where a head start in video counts for a lot.
Closing
For the closing, three numbers would settle most of what this piece leaves open about the sector:
How many takes get used? The only figures we have are 4% to 5% for the Kalshi ad and 25% for one animated episode. My personal conviction is that consistency will move this number more than raw quality will, which is what labs will lean towards: an environment which manages consistent context heavy generations rather than a single great one.
What does a finished hour really cost? Divide the list price by the share of takes kept. On today’s prices, the same hour of video can cost:
Does the physics hold? Physics-IQ is the only public test of whether models move like the real world, and the best model scores about half of what real footage does, the gap closes first where a model has real footage to build on.
Two years ago, the question was whether AI video would ever look good enough. That question is mostly settled. The Kalshi ad aired during the NBA Finals, and Netflix put generated footage in a finished show.
The open questions now are about money and control:
Who gets paid? Studios want a cut or a royalty-esque mechanism whenever their characters appear. Licensed fan creation of characters, individuals or idols can see a lot of growth.
What becomes possible? If the physics gap closes, video models stop being clip makers and become simulators. Our call: the first paying overlap will be robot training, where a model continues real camera footage. That is the setup where scores are already highest (63 against 50), and Runway’s GWM-1 already sells into it. Games come later, because they need a model to start from nothing and stay consistent for hours. Through 2027, we expect the simulator market to stay smaller than the ad and production market it grows out of. The call is wrong if a game studio ships a title built on a generated world model before then.
Company figures are as stated, press figures as reported, estimates labelled, and calculations ours. List prices read 20 October 2026; Google's and Runway's, the Artificial Analysis leaderboard (v2.1) and Physics-IQ read 2 November. ReelShort figures are Media Partners Asia estimates via Indian Television; Owl & Co shares via The Hollywood Reporter, checked against a secondary summary; Meta and Ormax figures are Meta's published survey. Why Meta’s Andromeda Update Just Killed Lazy AI Ad Variations (And the Workflow Replacing It)
Most DTC brands think they’re testing 40 ads a month.
Meta’s retrieval engine looks at your account, sees 1 ad, and punishes you for it.
On October 28, 2026, Meta’s engineering team quietly published the technical breakdown of its next-generation Andromeda ad retrieval architecture. If you run paid social—or edit video ads for brands that do—this is the single most important update of the year.
Here is what actually changed under the hood, why superficial AI ad variations stopped scaling, and how to restructure your creative pipeline around it.
1. What Meta’s Retrieval Engine Actually Does Now
Every time someone opens Facebook or Instagram, Meta filters millions of eligible ads down to a tiny shortlist before ranking ever happens. That first filter is Andromeda.
In its October 2026 upgrade, Meta co-designed its retrieval models directly onto NVIDIA GPU pipelines. The production system now evaluates over 1 billion ads per second—a 100x jump over the 2024 architecture—using a Retrieval Mixture-of-Experts model that approaches full ranking-level quality at the very first gate.
Meta explicitly stated why they built this: generative AI tools and Advantage+ automation flooded the auction with hundreds of millions of new ad assets.
When everyone can generate 50 variants in ten minutes, the bottleneck shifts from making ads to matching genuinely distinct creative angles to distinct buyer personas.
2. Cosmetic Volume vs. Conceptual Diversity
Here is where most media buyers and creative teams are bleeding margin right now:
They take one winning talking-head video, swap the first 3-second text hook, change the background color, export 15 crops, and call it "high-velocity creative testing."
Andromeda’s retrieval towers don't treat those as 15 different entry points. Same face, same visual world, same core argument = one creative entity competing for the exact same pocket of attention. Meanwhile, Meta's average price per ad jumped 14% year-over-year in Q3 2026. Paying 14% higher CPMs to show the same idea in five different fonts is a fast way to tank contribution margin.
Andromeda rewards conceptual diversity:
Different buyer personas and entry hooks
Different visual environments and formats (unboxing vs. problem demonstration vs. contrarian split-screen)
Different psychological angles for buying
3. How to Use AI Video Properly for Andromeda
The mistake isn't using AI for ad production. The mistake is using AI to make copies instead of new worlds.
If you have one winning script or core product benefit, here is the 3-step workflow to turn it into 5 genuinely distinct concepts in 48 hours:
Lock the Product & Voice First: Start with clean product reference frames and a real human voiceover (or a high-cadence script). Dual-stream models like Veo 3, Kling, and Runway Gen-4.5 hold lip-sync and ambient pacing far better when audio cadence drives the generation rather than retrofitting voiceover onto random silent clips.
Build 5 Distinct Visual Hooks Around One Angle: Instead of changing caption colors, change the visual reality of the first 3 seconds:
Concept A: Raw handheld bathroom-mirror testimonial
Concept B: Macro studio product-physics shot
Concept C: High-contrast split-screen comparison
Concept D: Founder/expert breakdown with b-roll overlays
Concept E: Specific lifestyle "moment of use" scene
Cut for Retention in Post: Never upload raw generative outputs straight to Ads Manager. Bring the clips into Premiere or DaVinci, tighten every dead 4-frame pause, layer native typography, and ensure the product geometry stays 100% faithful.
Meta built an engine capable of matching a billion ads a second. Stop feeding it 20 versions of the same video. Feed it 5 completely different reasons to care.

Our AI host Mira made a full K-pop music video in one night.
4 performers. 3 sets. 14 shots. 60 seconds. Hindi and English.
Made with Soundverse. Here is every step, the exact prompts, and the real token bill.
Quick disclosure: Mira is an AI host created for Soundverse. Her face, voice and studio are AI-generated. So are the four performers and the three sets.
The stack
Agent One: voice clone and the song
Stem Separator: vocals and instrumental
AI Video Generator with Seedance 2.5: every shot
Music Video Lip Sync: the verses
AI Studio: the edit
1. Clone the voice
Open Agent One. Drop in 30 seconds of talking, some English, some Hindi.
Type one line: "clone this voice and name it Mira."
9 seconds later, the voice is saved.
2. Generate the song
Paste the lyrics with section tags. Add a style: desi pop with K-pop polish, a four-member girl group, Hindi and English, a hook the whole arena can chant.
Then ask Agent One to generate the song in the cloned voice. It plans every step.
A couple of minutes later, the song is ready.
3. Split the stems
Stem Separator, 2 stems.
The vocals will drive the lip sync. The instrumental will drive the dance.
Two files, two jobs.
4. Lock the cast before any video
This is where most AI music videos fall apart. Faces drift between shots.
The fix: make every face first, as a sharp close-up. Then build the full stage look from that face.
Noor, the rapper. Tara, the main vocalist. Kavya, the visual. And Mira.
Three sets: a sold-out arena, a chrome mirror corridor, a rooftop over Mumbai at night.
 
 
5. Shoot every scene on Seedance 2.5
AI Tools, then AI Video Generator, then Seedance 2.5. Seedance 2.0, Veo 3.1 and Gemini Omni Flash 1.1 sit in the same menu.
The formula:
One clear direction: one camera move, the light, who is in frame
Reference images: her face, her stage look, the set
Reference audio: that line from the vocal stem, so she sings it
5 seconds, 16:9, 720p (480p and 1080p are in the menu)
The real prompt for Tara's verse:
"Tara, our main vocalist, sings in a chrome mirror corridor. Keep her face, curls and ivory-gold corset dress exactly as in the references. She sings the reference audio, lips synced to every word, then turns slowly so the organza train swirls, and the mirrors multiply her. Medium close-up, slow arc. Cool silver light, warm light on her face."
The panel shows the cost before you hit Generate: 3,330 tokens for 5 seconds.
 
 
6. Make the group dance in sync
Real girl groups have one signature move. So give yours one, and describe it exactly.
Ours: tap your wrist like a watch, then one finger to the sky. Ek minute.
The trick: attach the INSTRUMENTAL as reference audio. Every move lands on the beat.
Then tell them not to sing:
"All four members dance the chorus in PERFECT SYNC to the beat of the reference audio. Signature move: left hand taps the right wrist like a watch, then the right arm shoots up, one finger to the sky. NOBODY SINGS: lips closed the whole time. Mumbai rooftop at night, medium-wide, slow arc."
Loose lip sync on four faces looks bad. Closed mouths look like a real performance.
 
 
7. Lock the lips on the verses
Music Video Lip Sync, run from Agent One. Attach the shot and its vocal line:
"Lip sync this shot to this vocal line with Music Video Lip Sync. Keep everything else exactly the same."
It redraws only the mouth. Same shot, same face, same light. One face per shot. 100 tokens a second.
Use it when one singer faces the camera. Skip it when hands or hair cross the face. On a tight close-up we saw a seam on the cheek, so that shot went back to closed mouths.
 
8. Cut it in AI Studio
The song goes on the timeline, with a jump to the final chorus, so the story fits in 60 seconds.
Every shot goes on the video lane, cut on the beat. At 106 BPM, two bars is about 4.5 seconds, so 5-second shots trim cleanly.
One colour grade and a little film grain on top.
 
The bill
What it actually cost: 148,570 Soundverse tokens. Lots of mistakes, and very picky with every output.
If everything works first time, about 55,150:
Voice clone: 6,000
Song: 500
Stem split: 200
14 shots on Seedance 2.5 at 720p with references (666 tokens a second): 45,954
Music Video Lip Sync on 5 verses: 2,500
Video is about 83% of the clean-run bill, and retakes are where it grows. Lock the cast and the audio slices before you shoot.
(Soundverse tokens only. The cast and set stills were made before the shoot and aren't in either number.)
 
The short version
Faces first, then looks from the faces
One signature move, described exactly
Vocal slice as reference audio for singing shots
Instrumental as reference audio for dance shots, with "nobody sings"
Lip sync only one face that faces the camera
Cut on the bar

The proof: a 31-second AI clip, 322K likes, 15M views
 
This is a 31-second, fully AI-generated clip. Instagram even shows the "AI" label in the corner. Here's what it pulled:
322K likes
31.4K shares
5,782 reposts
1,163 comments
The number that matters is shares. 31.4K sends is about 1 share for every 10 likes, which is a lot. Sends are one of the strongest signals Instagram uses to push a reel to new people. People aren't only liking this; they're DMing it to their partner with "this is us."
And it isn't a one-off. Vintage, 90s-rom-com-style AI "episodes" with the same recurring couple are all over Reels right now. The audience knows they're AI and doesn't care, because the story lands.
The good news: this format is very repeatable. Once your characters are locked, every new episode is a script and one generation. Here's the full workflow, with every prompt, and how to run all of it inside HeyOz without hopping between five tools.
Why these work (steal the anatomy, not the video)
Break the reel down and you find the same five parts every time:
A look that feels like a memory. 35mm grain, warm tungsten light, soft glow on the highlights, creamy ivory and navy palette. It reads as "a 90s movie you half-remember," not "AI video."
An aspirational world. A Manhattan penthouse, snow outside the window, silk robes, espresso in china cups. Viewers love watching it.
Two gorgeous, consistent characters. Same faces, same signature wardrobe, every episode. Consistency turns a one-off clip into a show people come back for.
A 30-second story with a reversal. In the reference reel: she shaves his beard while he sleeps → he wakes up, finds it gone → deadpan confrontation ("It was a caterpillar.") → he gets revenge and smudges her mascara → she draws a mustache on him → both laughing. That's setup → reaction → counter-move → affectionate payoff.
Almost no dialogue. Lines are 2–5 words, with small burned-in subtitles. The faces do the comedy. Short lines also keep AI lip-sync clean.
That's the formula. Now let's build it.
The workflow at a glance
Write the episode (premise + 6–8 beats)
Define your characters in a character bible
Generate character reference sheets and lock them
Submit the sheets + your shot-by-shot prompt to the video model
Add subtitles, post, repeat with the same cast
In HeyOz, steps 3 and 4 happen in the same workspace. Your sheets are saved once and reused for every episode, with no downloading and re-uploading between an image tool and a video tool.
Step 1: Write the episode
Every episode follows one structure:
Setup (0–8s): one character does something cheeky
Discovery (8–15s): the other finds out → tight deadpan close-up
Counter-move (15–24s): they get even
Payoff (24–30s): both break and laugh, or a hug. Always end warm, never mean.
Rules: max 4 lines of dialogue, max 5 words per line, every beat visual. If a moment only works with a long sentence, rewrite it.
Use this prompt in any LLM to generate episodes:
 
The example episode we build in this guide:
"The Last Croissant." Jack hides the last croissant in his newspaper. Margot sees him in the mirror, sneaks a huge bite, folds it back. He finds the bite. "Something bit my croissant." She doesn't look up: "Mice." He drains her coffee in one go. "Mice." She throws a napkin at him; both lose it laughing.
Step 2: Define your characters
This is the step everyone skips, and it's why their characters drift into different people by shot three.
Write a character bible: one paragraph per character, specific enough that two different artists would draw the same person. Cover age, build, face, hair, skin, eyes, signature wardrobe, accessories, and personality (personality drives the acting).
 
Two tips:
Never prompt with celebrity names. It's against most platforms' rules, and invented faces are easier to keep consistent anyway.
Give each character one signature costume. Same pajamas every episode works like a cartoon character's outfit: instant recognition in the feed.
Step 3: Generate and lock your character reference sheets
A reference sheet shows the same character from every angle with several expressions, all on one image. The video model studies it to keep the face, hair and wardrobe identical in every shot.
In HeyOz: open the image generator and pick a high-detail model. GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max detail) or Nano Banana Pro (strongest prompt adherence) work best for sheets. Everything you generate is saved to your assets, ready for Step 4.
3a. Generate the hero portrait first
Don't start with the full sheet. Lock the face first, generate 4–6 options, and pick the one you love.
 
3b. Build the sheet from that portrait
Attach the chosen portrait as a reference image and run:
 
Repeat for the second character.
3c. Two extra sheets that save you hours
The couple scale shot fixes height and size differences so he doesn't shrink between shots. Attach both sheets:
 
The location sheet keeps the set consistent across episodes:
 
Lock it. Look at every sheet zoomed in. If the face changes between panels, regenerate now. Every flaw in a sheet repeats in every episode.
Step 4: Submit the sheets + your prompt to the video model
This is where most people lose an hour: download sheets from one tool, upload them to another, lose track of which version was final.
In HeyOz: open the video generator, choose Seedance 2.5, and attach your sheets straight from your assets. Seedance 2.5 on HeyOz takes up to 30 reference images, generates up to 30 seconds in one go, outputs 9:16, and generates native audio, so dialogue and room sound come baked in.
Settings: Seedance 2.5 · 9:16 · 30s · 1080p · audio on. Use 720p while you're testing beats.
Attach your references in this order. In the prompt, refer to each one by its tag:
@image1: Jack's reference sheet
@image2: Margot's reference sheet
@image3: Location sheet
@image4: Couple scale shot
The master style block (reuse it every episode)
 
The full episode prompt: "The Last Croissant"
 
If a 30-second take drifts
One long take is fastest, but if a character drifts mid-clip, split the episode into three ~10-second generations. Use the same references and style block, and describe only those shots. Start each segment's prompt with where the last one ended ("Continuing: Jack is standing at the table holding the newspaper…"). Then stitch them together.
Still one bad moment? Re-roll just that segment, or fix it with Seedance 2.5 video edit right inside HeyOz instead of regenerating the whole clip.
Step 5: Subtitles, posting and turning it into a series
Subtitles: small, white, clean sans-serif, centered just below the middle of the frame, one line at a time. Add them in your editor rather than in the prompt, because AI-rendered text garbles.
Music (optional): a quiet vintage jazz-piano bed under the dialogue suits the look.
Caption: "Ep. 12 — The Last Croissant" style numbering tells viewers it's a show and gets them to follow for the next one.
Same cast, every episode. Your sheets are already sitting in HeyOz, so episode 2 is just a new script + one generation.
10 premises to start with:
She hides his car keys in the freezer; he hides her heels in the fridge
He secretly swaps her perfume for vanilla extract
The thermostat war: up, down, up, both in coats
He "lets her win" at chess, then she checkmates him for real
She tapes a "WET PAINT" sign on his favorite armchair
He wears her silk robe to fetch the newspaper
Pillow-fort standoff on a snow day
She tells him the soufflé is "just for looking"; he eats it anyway
He shrinks her sweater on purpose; she wears it as a crop top and wins
Who-can-stay-silent-longest bet, ruined by a sneeze
Common problems and fixes
Faces drift between shots: add more angles to the sheet, restate "keep faces exactly as in the reference sheets" in the cast line, and keep shots to 2 characters max.
Looks too modern / too "AI": reinforce "35mm film, grain, halation, natural skin texture" and "no modern objects."
Lip-sync is off: shorten the line. 2–5 words syncs cleanly; full sentences don't.
Weird hands on props: keep prop handling simple (one object, one hand) and avoid tiny detailed tasks in close-up.
The joke doesn't land: you're probably missing the deadpan close-up. The pause on the reaction face is the punchline.
Why we build these in HeyOz
The usual stack for this format: an LLM for the script → an image tool for the sheets → download → a different video tool → upload → re-upload when you fix a sheet → repeat for every episode.
In HeyOz, it's one workspace:
Top image models in one place for character and location sheets: GPT Image 2.6, Nano Banana Pro, Midjourney, Seedream 5 Pro
Top video models in one place: Seedance 2.5 (30s, up to 30 references, native audio), Kling 4, Veo 3.1 and more, so you can run the same episode on two models and keep the better one
Your sheets live in your assets. Generate once, attach to every future episode in one click
One credit balance instead of four subscriptions
Script it, cast it, shoot it, fix it, all without leaving one tab. Make your first episode at heyoz.com, then reply with what you made. We'll repost the best ones.
